Sware
swâr
v. (past tense of swear; rendering Hebrew shaba', Greek omosen)
The older strong past tense of swear, from Saxon swor; modern English has levelled it to swore. Hebrew shaba' is built on the number seven, and to swear was literally to seven oneself — the sacred number invoked in the binding of a promise.

Biblical Definition

Sware is the old past of swear, and Scripture uses it of oaths between men and, more weightily, of God's own oath. Abraham and Abimelech settle a dispute over a well and name the place for what happened there: “he called that place Beersheba; because there they sware both of them” (Genesis 21:31). Jacob binds Joseph about his burial (Genesis 47:31). David, who could have destroyed Saul in the cave, instead swears to spare his house: “And David sware unto Saul” (1 Samuel 24:22). Asa's reformation is sealed by a national oath taken aloud: “they sware unto the LORD with a loud voice, and with shouting, and with trumpets, and with cornets” (2 Chronicles 15:14). But the most consequential oaths in Scripture are God's. He swore to the fathers to give the land; He swore in His wrath that a generation should not enter His rest (Numbers 32:10); and He swore by Himself to Abraham, because He could swear by no greater — which is the argument of Hebrews 6 for the immutability of His counsel.

Webster 1828 Definition

The older past tense of swear, now levelled to swore. In Scripture it records oaths between men — at Beersheba, in the cave, at Asa's reformation — and above all the oath of God, who swore by Himself because He could swear by no greater.

SWARE, v. [Sax. swor.] The past tense of swear; now more commonly swore.

2. To affirm or promise with a solemn appeal to God for the truth of the declaration.

3. To bind oneself by oath; as, David sware unto Saul.

4. The Hebrew shaba' is from sheba', seven; to swear was to seven oneself, invoking the sacred number.

5. In Scripture, there they sware both of them, Gen. 21; they sware unto the LORD with a loud voice, 2 Chron. 15.

Key Scripture

Genesis 47:31 — "And he said, Swear unto me. And he sware unto him. And Israel bowed himself upon the bed's head."

1 Samuel 24:22 — "And David sware unto Saul. And Saul went home; but David and his men gat them up unto the hold."

2 Chronicles 15:14 — "And they sware unto the LORD with a loud voice, and with shouting, and with trumpets, and with cornets."

Numbers 32:10 — "And the LORD'S anger was kindled the same time, and he sware, saying,"

Modern Corruption

God's oath is sometimes treated as a mere figure of speech, since God cannot lie and therefore needs no oath. Hebrews takes it the other way: the oath was added not because His word required support but because our weakness required comfort.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is the ground of assurance in God's sworn promise. Hebrews 6 reasons that men swear by the greater, and an oath for confirmation is to them an end of all strife; wherefore God, willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of His counsel, confirmed it by an oath. Two immutable things follow — the promise and the oath — in both of which it was impossible for God to lie. The doubling is not for God's sake but for ours, that we might have strong consolation.

The same passage rebukes an assurance sought elsewhere. Believers commonly look for confidence in the strength of their own believing, and so rise and fall with their frames. The anchor Hebrews describes is fixed within the veil, where the forerunner is for us entered; it is Christ's presence there and God's sworn word that hold, not the vigour of the grip. Numbers 32:10 shows the other edge of the same attribute: God also swears in wrath, and what He swears then is equally unalterable. An oath from God settles a matter permanently in whichever direction it points.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shaba', to swear, derives from sheba', seven; hence Beersheba, the well of the oath or of seven. Greek omnuo is to swear, and horkos is the oath itself.

expand to see more

Hebrew shaba' (H7650) — to swear, to adjure; literally to seven oneself, to bind by the sacred number.

Hebrew sheba' (H7651) — seven; the root behind both swearing and the name Beersheba.

Greek omnuo (G3660) — to swear, to take an oath; its aorist omosen is used of God in Hebrews 6:13.

Greek horkos (G3727) — an oath; that which confirms a promise and ends strife among men.

Saxon swor — the Old English past of swerian, to swear.

Usage

"Of an oath that named a place: he called that place Beersheba; because there they sware both of them (Genesis 21:31)."

"Of mercy sworn to an enemy: And David sware unto Saul (1 Samuel 24:22)."

"Of a national covenant renewed aloud: they sware unto the LORD with a loud voice (2 Chronicles 15:14)."
